data.title: Skalka nad Váhom – a hillfort and a vampire grave above the Váh
data.excerpt: The Chochel promontory above the confluence of the Súčianka with the Váh overlooks the Trenčín Gate, the narrowest point of the Váh valley. The site was occupied from the Maďarovce culture through the Celts to Germanic peoples, and in the second half of the 9th century a tiny church – probably of timber, with a nave of just 14.8 m² – was built on it. Inside it lay a grave whose skull had been removed and whose chest was weighted down with eleven stones.
data.metaTitle: Skalka nad Váhom – hillfort at the Trenčín Gate
data.metaDescription: A hillfort on the Chochel promontory above the Váh near Trenčín, with the footings of a tiny early medieval church and a vampire grave inside it.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: The Trenčín Gate; the “Chochel” promontory on the hill of Skalka above the confluence of the Súčianka with the Váh

keyFacts.label: Dimensions of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: Length 192 m, width 23–39 m, total area 0.55 ha

keyFacts.label: Relative height

keyFacts.label: Local tradition
keyFacts.value: Local people believed that a pagan sanctuary – the “Temple of Venus” – stood on the hill

keyFacts.label: Church building
keyFacts.value: Nave and apse measuring 5.3 × 5.4–5.6 m (6.2 m including the apse); the nave covers only 14.8 m²

keyFacts.label: Vampire grave
keyFacts.value: A grave uncovered inside the sanctuary, with the skull removed afterwards and the chest weighted down with eleven stones

keyFacts.label: Benedictine abbey
keyFacts.value: Founded in 1224 by Jakub, Bishop of Nitra, 800 m from the church building on Chochel

keyFacts.label: Archaeological excavation
keyFacts.value: First digs in 1889–1890, further work in the 1930s and a detailed excavation in 1995 during motorway construction

timeline.description: A group of six graves of the 9th–10th centuries arose behind the apse of the church building; among them was a grave with anti-vampire practices carried out afterwards (the skull removed, the body weighted down with eleven stones).

children.text: One of the most striking geographical divides in the region of the middle Váh is the Trenčín Gate. It is the narrowest point of the Váh valley, bounded by the castle rock of Trenčín and by the hill of Skalka. The massif of Skalka, on the right bank of the Váh, descends gradually and almost regularly from its summit towards its outer sides. The exception is a promontory that juts out into the river floodplain above the confluence of the Súčianka with the Váh. This formation, 570 m from the summit of Skalka, has the narrow shape of a ridge. In local usage the hill came to be known as “Chochel”.

From its northern, north-western and south-eastern margins the slopes of the hill fall away steeply, dropping more than 70 m to its foot. The gently descending terrain between the summit of Skalka and the site was already divided at its narrowest point in prehistory by an artificially heaped rampart. The natural defensibility thus reinforced turned the site into a reliably defensible fortified hilltop settlement 192 m long, 23–39 m wide, with a total area of 0.55 ha.

The first excavation work at the site dates to 1889–1890. The artefacts found – a bone stylus, a Roman brooch and pottery fragments – were sold to Vienna together with other finds. The insights gained nevertheless placed the site on the Chochel hill among the important find spots of prehistoric remains in the surroundings of Trenčín. Among the local population the belief took hold that a pagan sanctuary – the “Temple of Venus” – had stood here in ancient times. During excavation of the site in the 1930s, interesting artefacts came to light, such as larger S-shaped temple rings and finger rings (made of a rod, of a band, with a bezel, with an eyelet). They were accompanied by beads, small crosses, coins, knives, fishing spears, buckles and a small whetstone, a bearded axe, bronze pins, brooches, pot-shaped vessels, sherds, spindle whorls, a small chain, a razor and a glass bracelet. In 1995, when a motorway was under construction in the immediate vicinity, a detailed excavation began at the site. The excavation produced many finds from several periods of the past, specifically from the Bronze Age, the Early Historical period and the Middle Ages.
The Bronze Age

The earliest occupation of the site on the Chochel hill can broadly be assigned to the end of the Early and the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age. It is represented by a fortification, settlement features and items of material culture. The fortification

is situated on the south-western edge of the site, where the neck of the promontory joins the sloping terrain of Skalka. Its original body was destroyed by fire and subsequently decayed naturally. In the Early Historical period it was functionally incorporated into the body of a new fortification and covered by a considerable volume of freshly heaped earth. The stabilising element of the core of the rampart was a grillage construction. Besides the rampart, fragments of several settlement features have survived from the Bronze Age. As regards items of material culture, pottery finds dominate, attested by almost a thousand fragments. The typological range of vessels is characteristic of the Maďarovce culture. Only a minimum of bronze tools was found. It can therefore be concluded that the fortified settlement on the Chochel hill was occupied during the classic phase of the Maďarovce culture, which fills the peak of the Early Bronze Age, and during the Late Maďarovce phase at the beginning of the Middle Bronze Age. It was in the course of the latter that the fortification on the south-western edge of the site was destroyed by fire. The function of the settlement described here is still unknown, as are the reasons that led to its construction. In all probability economic aspects were not decisive in this respect. Given the location of a more important contemporary fortified settlement on the castle rock of Trenčín, it is doubtful that anything would have prompted the need to build another administrative centre in its immediate vicinity. More plausible are considerations of a refuge function in the border zone of the settled oikumene of the Maďarovce culture, reinforced by a possible need to protect the route leading along the Vlára valley towards the mountain pass.

children.text: The Early Historical period

The second phase of occupation of the Chochel hill, belonging to the Early Historical period, can be divided into three phases, or broad time spans: the Late La Tène to the Early Roman period, the Early Roman period and the Late Roman period. Traces of the activities of the population in these spans can be observed in the fortification, in the settlement features and in the material culture.

In the Early Historical period, during the Late La Tène, the older fortification from the first phase of occupation was brought back into use. In the territory of present-day Slovakia this period is associated with the Celtic population. A method known and repeatedly applied in the past was used. Its principle is the construction of a new, more massive body designed so that the older fortification is also put to practical use within it. In accordance with this concept, the earth sliding down the slope from the body of the first-phase rampart was levelled in front of it. This level was then covered with a 15–18 cm thick layer of sandy loam mixed with angular gravel, which may have had both an insulating and a drainage function. The lower end of this layer was recorded in front of the edge of the ditch. Above its upper end a grillage construction was built. In section it reached a width of about 3 m. Within a span of less than a metre, traces of five vertically placed wooden beams were recorded in its profile. The construction was filled mainly with light-yellow subsoil loam and, sporadically, with small and medium-sized stones. Along the edges of the front and rear faces it was supplemented with rods. These rods were laid obliquely to the transverse line, at an angle of about 45–50°. The front of the grillage construction was protected by a wall of stones bonded with clay. Only its lowest foundation level, made of large and medium-sized stones, has survived. The crown of the defensive wall may have been finished with a timber superstructure. In front of the wall lay a ditch. The Late La Tène fortification was destroyed by a massive fire. The function of the hillfort was in all probability restored during the next phase of occupation. There was no extensive rebuilding of the original structure, only a limited modification of its existing state. As regards settlement features, storage pits were the most frequently represented at the site. Remains of oval huts were also recorded, which have only rarely been documented at the settlements in Branč and Veľký Meder.

The most intensive occupation of the Chochel hill is recorded in the Early Historical period, especially from the Late La Tène to the Early Roman period. The period of the Púchov culture in particular is richly represented. This occupation is represented by numerous sherds of pottery typical of that period. Among the small objects from the Early Historical period, the most numerous are spindle whorls of various shapes and elongated whetstones made of river pebbles. Chronologically more sensitive are fragments of agricultural tools, supplemented by a razor with a semicircular edge, part of a blue glass bracelet with oblique plastic ribs and part of a pair of spring shears. Further finds include a bronze brooch of the Alesia type, a brooch with a bent bow made of an iron rod, a bronze bracelet with transverse grooves and an iron omega-shaped brooch, a bronze brooch of the Almgren type and a fragment of a bronze belt clasp of the early Noric-Pannonian type. The knife with an arched back and the socketed spearhead are also of interest.

The agricultural orientation of the population is confirmed not only by the iron tools, but also by the storage pits and by the composition of the animal bones recovered from the features and from the occupation layer. Most come from domestic animals, above all sheep, cattle and goats. Among the wild animals there were red deer, aurochs and wild boar. Traces of gnawing by dogs were noted on some bones; other marks must be connected with the human processing of the meat parts of animals, including roasting. Pronounced marks on red deer antlers attest to an effort to put them to primarily practical use. Not all pieces of antler came from hunted animals. The collecting of shed antlers was not unusual either. The composition of the wild animals suggests that the surroundings of the site may have been covered by an open mixed woodland. The find of beaver bones and of the shells of river molluscs, used as a supplementary source of meat food, must be linked with the proximity of the watercourse.

The destruction of the Late La Tène fortification by a massive fire in the Early Roman period can be connected with the arrival of Germanic peoples, and in the same way a number of fortified enclosures of the Púchov culture were affected. Through their actions the occupation was reduced, which was subsequently followed by a retreat northwards – from the Trenčín micro-region into the Púchov area. During the Early Roman period the vacated space was gradually filled by settlements of the Germanic Quadi.

After the territory had been occupied by Germanic peoples, especially at the time of the Marcomannic Wars against the Roman Empire, the hillfort was occupied again, because the site was easy to defend.
The Middle Ages – the Slavs
From the Early Middle Ages, when the Váh region was inhabited by the Slavs, come several settlement features, a church building, items of material culture and a necropolis.

The first of the two Slavic features investigated is a sunken-featured building, a dwelling with its floor sunk into a pit, situated below the north-western edge of the slumping body of the Early Historical rampart, next to the access route to the site. Its long axis runs parallel to the line of steepest slope of the sloping terrain. It is 4.4 m long and sunk 1.7–1.9 m deep. Of its presumed width of 3 m, a stretch of 1.9 m was recorded. Along the perimeter of the southern sector two post holes were found, whose posts had been set into the faces of the walls in order to ensure stability. Two levels of compact floor daub testify to a longer-term use of the feature during the 9th–10th centuries. The second feature is the burnt daub of the firing chamber of a domed oven from the central part of the site, dating to the 11th–12th centuries.
The foundations of the sanctuary

In the central part of the site, at the intersection of its long and transverse axes, a church building was erected. It consisted of a nave of irregular square plan and a shallowly curved semicircular apse. Its external dimensions are given as 5.3 × 5.4–5.6 m, or 6.2 m including the apse. The long axis of the building, running through the centre of the apse, is oriented SE–NW and is thus deflected by 43° from the sacred axis laid out on an E–W line. On the southern side two square projections abut the wall; they are probably the remains of the foundations of a neck-like porch covering the entrance portal.

The building has survived in the form of one to two lowest courses of foundation masonry, built of quarried stone of local provenance bonded with mortar. In some stretches of the perimeter masonry the stones were bonded only with clay. The interior floor was paved with thin flat sandstone slabs in the manner of terracotta tiling. The complete absence of stone in the surroundings of the church raises doubts that its perimeter walls, and possibly also the porch over the entrance portal, were built of this material. Had that been the case, the volume involved would not have been negligible; it can be estimated at more than 30 m³. The excavation, however, did not recover even fragments of mortar binder, which would have remained on the spot even if the masonry had been dismantled and the stones transported for secondary use elsewhere. It therefore cannot be ruled out that the walls of the church building were built of timber. The concentrated occurrence of iron cramps and nails around the church building is likewise among the evidence for the use of timber and for the structural joining of some of its parts. The course of the foundation masonry revealed by the excavation recalls the stone footings of timber churches, which were built in both the Early and the High Middle Ages using various techniques. From the 10th–12th centuries such buildings are attested in neighbouring Austria and Poland, but in greater numbers in the countries of western and northern Europe. In most cases they were temporary places of worship, replaced after some time by stone ones. Milan Hanuliak states that the church was probably built as early as the period of Great Moravia. This is demonstrated by a number of circumstances, such as the siting of the building, which was commonly used in the 9th century but does not occur at the time when church architecture was developing in the Hungarian state in the 11th and 12th centuries.

children.text: Dating the construction of the church building back to the 9th century is also supported by the concentration of characteristic pottery finds in its immediate surroundings and by the group of six graves of the 9th–10th centuries placed behind its apse. Within this chronological framework – unlike the sacred canon governing the orientation of the long axis of High Medieval churches – the deviation of the building under analysis from the orientation used in the later period is not quite so inadmissible. The question of the function of the uncovered building is closely bound up with some of these circumstances. The total area of the nave, 14.8 m², can hardly have been intended for a larger group of worshippers. In this detail one may perhaps also see an expression of cultic archaism, in which the church building is regarded as the dwelling of God and those attending the service stand outside it.

It is remarkable that this building, despite the archaic nature of the peculiarities recorded (plan, dimensions, absence of an altar mensa and probably also the timber construction of the walls), had the attributes of a parish church in the period from the 11th to the 13th century. This is attested not only by the churchyard cemetery, but also by a written mention of the parish priest from the village of Skala, who later entered the Benedictine abbey founded at Skalka in 1224. Since the serf estate of the parish passed into the property of the monastery together with him, it is clear that the church building ceased to fulfil its former functions, fell into decay and was abandoned. In the same way, burial in the churchyard cemetery probably declined and later ceased altogether.

All the circumstances surrounding this small church on the hillfort are something of a mystery. Was it of stone or of timber? Does it date from the time of Great Moravia, or was it built only when church architecture was developing in the Kingdom of Hungary? Was it a Christian building at all, or did a pagan temple originally stand here, one that survived in the memory of the common people as the “Temple of Venus” mentioned at the beginning? Why would anyone build a church on a hillfort that bears several signs of a refuge rather than anything else, when a central hillfort stood a few kilometres from Skalka on the site of today’s Trenčín Castle? The greatest mystery of all, however, remains the vampire grave found inside the sanctuary.
A vampire in the sanctuary on the hillfort

At first glance, the case of the individual from the grave placed inside the church building might recall the application of the principle enshrined in the “Legis Salicae”, according to which a church was to be built over the grave of an important individual. However, the dead person from the interior of the sanctuary on the Skalka hillfort can hardly have belonged to the contemporary category of more important individuals, because anti-vampire practices had been carried out on the body, including the subsequent removal of the head and the weighting of the upper part of the torso with eleven stones. As has been mentioned, the skeleton lacked the skull and five cervical vertebrae, which had been removed from the grave afterwards.

Manifestations of this kind are referred to in the territory of present-day Slovakia as posterior anti-vampire practices and were carried out above all at cemeteries outside churches, where several lingering expressions of the pagan rite survived. From Great Moravia we know of several cases of so-called vampire graves, in which individuals were mutilated after death, or rather after burial, for ritual reasons – above all by the removal of one of the limbs or of the head, or by being weighted down with large boulders. The purpose of these practices may have been, for example, to ensure that the dead person could not rise from the grave and do evil to the living.
Medieval finds

The group of settlement finds is traditionally represented by pottery vessels and their fragments. They come from handmade pot-shaped forms with a wheel-finished upper part covered with a range of decorative motifs characteristic of the 9th–10th centuries. On the basis of their find spot, a ring-shaped earring of bronze wire, a bronze
gombík

and an arrowhead with backward barbs must also be counted among the settlement finds of the 9th–10th centuries. The rhomboid and deltoid forms of arrowheads belong to the 10th–11th centuries. Among the other finds, a sheet-metal strap end, the goad of a spur, a fish hook, an iron knife and a bone whistle, beads of mother-of-pearl-coloured glass and a band-shaped finger ring with longitudinal grooves may be mentioned. The earlier excavations (in the 1930s) yielded knives, a pot-shaped vessel, a bearded axe, a sandstone whetstone and a tongue-shaped bronze belt strap end. A few further finds come from the 11th and 12th centuries, when the site was used as a cemetery. Several finger rings and items of women’s jewellery were found. The coins form a separate group of finds. Of their qualities, their dating capacity deserves particular appreciation. Two of the originally seven excavated pieces are Hungarian anonymous denarii from the beginning of the 12th century. They support a more precise dating of the beginnings of burial in the cemetery.

Compared with the character of the prehistoric and Early Historical occupation of the Chochel hill, a transformation took place in the Middle Ages and the religious component came to the fore. Reasons so far unknown determined that this reliably defensible enclosure, with the typical features of Great Moravian refuge hillforts, was not more continuously occupied. In the course of the second half of the 9th century a timber church building of a specific plan was in all probability erected here, and burial began in the area behind its apse.

During the first three chronological spans (the Early Bronze Age, the Late La Tène period, the Early Roman period) the enclosure was used as a fortified hilltop settlement. Skalka, thanks to its position and in view of the proximity of the central hillfort at Trenčín Castle, a military and guard use and a refuge use, possibly supplemented by the duty of protecting one of the road routes leading towards the mountain pass.

Certainly not without a deeper connection is the distance of this site from the place where the Benedictine abbey was founded in 1224 by Jakub, Bishop of Nitra. It is a narrow terrace with a cave where, according to tradition, the monk Benedikt had his hermitage; he was later canonised together with Andrej (Svorad). The cave hermitage was ideally removed from the route of the busy Váh-valley road and from the newly built administrative centre on the castle hill of Trenčín. Moreover, it lies only 800 m from the church building on the Chochel hill, which is probably the oldest monument of its kind in the northern part of the middle Váh region.
